newsitem.title: BOSNIA: New Bosnian presidency unites to denounce bombing.
newsitem.headline: New Bosnian presidency unites to denounce bombing.

text.p: Bosnia's new inter-ethnic presidency on Friday condemned recent bombings of abandoned homes aimed at discouraging the return of war refugees and perpetuating territorial partition.
The statement made at the fourth meeting of the presidency was a significant expression of cooperation between its Moslem, Serb and Croat members, international peace officials said.

But the executive could not yet agree on who should be named chairman of a council of ministers to preside over a union of autonomous Moslem-Croat and Serb entities enshrined by a 1995 peace agreement.

Aides to Carl Bildt, the international peace coordinator in Bosnia, were nonetheless satisfied that the presidency was now convening regularly, twice a week, after weeks of haggling over the venue for sessions.

The presidency was elected on September 14 but meetings of all three members began only in late October after Serb nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik dropped his refusal to sign an oath of loyalty to a single state of Bosnia.

Friday's meeting was held in Sarajevo's National Museum, in Moslem-Croat Federation territory. The presidency's second session was in a suburb inside Serb republic territory. Meetings are to alternate between the two entities.

"They are moving forward merely by talking. They had substantive discussions. The fact they're meeting twice a week is absolutely extraordinary considering how recent the war was," Bildt spokesman Colum Murphy said.
The presidency members -- Moslem chairman Alija Izetbegovic, Krajisnik and Kresimir Zubak, a Croat, issued a joint statement decrying the spate of house bombings.

"The presidency sharply condemned all cases of destruction of houses in both the Federation and the Serb republic, and urged responsible authorities to take strong measures against any such actions," it said.

More than 150 homes that refugees expelled in the 1992-95 war had hoped to reoccupy under the Dayton peace treaty have been blown up by nationalist militants in recent days, most of them on Serb territory.
The statement said the presidency had discussed the composition of joint institutions, especially the council of ministers.
Krajisnik said after returning to the Serb Republic capital Pale near Sarajevo that disagreement surfaced at the meeting over the intended powers of the council of ministers.
"I must say we have gone a step backwards compared to the cooperativeness we had before in the work of joint bodies," the hardline Serb nationalist told reporters.
"Krajisnik's comments are normal," said a Bildt aide when asked whether his comments heralded obstruction by Serb separatists who accepted the Dayton peace treaty only under Western duress.
"After the first flush of getting these meetings going, things naturally slow down in the nitty-gritty of discussions. We see no step backwards."
Under the Dayton accords, the council of ministers is to consist of a chairman and at least two other members, a foreign minister and foreign trade minister.

Joint institutions are to govern by consensus. The constitution allows Serbs, Moslems or Croats to block measures they deem inimical to their vital interests, which in the eyes of some analysts is a recipe for political paralysis.
